comments.raw_comment:
1. This graph appears to show a correlation between a crime being committed with a gun and the likelihood of that crime being solved. From the graph we can see that a murders becomes less likely to be cleared as the likelihood of involvement of a gun increases. Another thing I noticed is that not every data point is labeled which I found to be a bit strange. 
2. I wonder if this is causation or just correlation. This could be interesting evidence showing that the more gun violence occurs the less justice is served (good title?) or maybe it shows the efficacy of the police force in these cities. I am not really sure but another thing that I wonder is how or why they chose these cities in particular. As I mentioned earlier, not every data point is labeled and I wonder if the cities are chosen by random, population or some other method. 
3.  Luckily Hawaii is not a place where violence is particularly common, especially gun violence. I believe that gun ownership hovers around 12-15% usually. Just out of interest with some quick research I put together a quick data point for Hawaii and found that in 2019 we had 32 homicides, 20 of which were solved giving us 62.5% of murders cleared. We had 62 gun related deaths in 2019 with around 66% being suicide and 23% being homicides (the other 11% probably being hunting related). Eventually we get 63% murders solved and about 43% of homicides with guns.https://efsgv.org/state/hawaii/https://projectcoldcase.org/cold-case-homicide-stats/

comments.raw_comment:
My headline: Who pulled the trigger?

First of all, the FBI and police agencies' report emphasizes how crimes with guns increase/decrease the possibility of a crime being solved. These can be seen, for example, in New York, which has a lower percentage of crimes committed with guns (less than 60%) but with more than 80% of crimes solved. While in cities where there are more gun crimes, such as Gary, Ind., with more than 90% of murders with guns, they have less than 20% of murders cleared.

Now, what factors could be influencing the likelihood of a gun murder being solved or not? This New York Times article likely wants to point to the controversial issue of gun laws in the United States, with variations in each state and many hidden conflicts of interest.

One of the main consequences of the poor gun restrictions is the impossibility of knowing who has access to guns, who owns them, and even if that person is physically and psychologically able to own a firearm. However, just a few months ago, Texas approved buying and carrying a gun without a license. While many applauded the fact, this evidence of graphics and data ends up being terrible news for this region. Guns make it challenging to solve a crime.

Finally, we can only hope that the government and the different states can reevaluate the gun control laws and come up with a solution that seeks the general welfare, not the profit of the gun industry in the country.

What do you notice?

I noticed how the New York Times got to pick which cities they wanted to graph. This is not a scientific study, but a political opinion trying to make it look like a scientific study. They created a trend line where places with less guns have a higher solving rate. Places with more guns have a lower solving rate. 

What do you wonder?

What is the motive behind this graph? I doubt science is behind it or the truth. I wonder why they are being dishonest and not trying to find the truth or put in all the data points and names of the cities?

How does this relate to you and your community?

This does not relate to my community because it is not named on the graph. What does relate is how the New York Times is trying to sway public opinion into removing guns out of the community. I live in a low income neighborhood with a high crime rate. If the government creates restrictions with guns then criminals will have guns and law abiding citizens will not.

comments.raw_comment: After viewing this graph, there are many things that can be noticed. To start, in cities with a larger percentage of murders done with guns, not as many murders were solved as those done without guns. This leads me to believe that murders done with guns are harder to solve, which can make these cities much more dangerous than cities with murders done without guns. While looking at this graph, I wonder how many murders were committed in each city each year on the graph. This would allow me to be able to understand which cities are safer regardless of murders done with or without guns. I also wonder which cities on the graph have more gun control. This would help readers understand how gun control can affect the crime rate in different cities. This relates to me because I have always wondered how the ownership and use of guns can affect crime in different cities. This can relate to my community because in America, many different citizens continuously argue about the use of guns. This allows people to have a better understand of how they affect society when used in the wrong way. In this graph, we see how murders committed with guns affect there chance of being solved. A catchy headline for this graph could be "more murders done with guns means more criminals on the run".

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, I notice that the likeliness of solving a murder that is involved with a gun is slim. I think this is because the type of combat that involves guns, in a sense, is not hand-to-hand combat. When people fire a gun it is something that is used from a distance. I wonder what kind of action the police force is taking because this is a problem. Innocent lives are being taken and the families of these victims don't even have the chance to know who caused their family pain. I also wonder what the government is doing about it. For the past few years now, the topic of gun restriction has been huge in America. Many groups of society believe that guns should be banned and I wonder if this topic of unsolved murders comes into the discussion. I also noticed that there are points on the graph that are not labeled and so I wonder what type of role they play in the graph. The town of Gary, Indiana has approximately 95% of murders that happen with guns. Out of this 95%, only about 5% were cleared. Maybe in smaller towns, it is harder to uncover crimes. This affects my community because I live only about 45 minutes from New York.  A catchy headline is "Who Can Solve the Case?"

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the increase of gun usage decreased the percentage of cleared murder cases.

What I'm curious about is the fact that gunshot murder cases would be harder to solve, when it should be relatively easy to find fingerprints on them. Also, they are bulkier than knives or a few other types of weapons, which would have made them more noticeable and the murderer easier to catch. comments.raw_comment: It does look like there may be an inverse relationship, but there is so much spread that it is hard to tell. This is partly because the population size is so big so that there is more room for variation. I think it's very interesting that the bigger counties are on the upper left hand of the graph. For example, Sacramento and New York, which have budgets of tens of billions of dollars. On the lower right side of the graph, we can see smaller counties like DeKalb and Gary, which have significantly lower budgets. This may confound the study because more prestigious detectives could be attracted to larger cities for larger salaries. Or cities with higher budgets could afford better detectives. I wonder how the data was collected and how long that took. I would be very interested to know the r value, or correlation, between the two variables to see how strong the relationship is. A residual plot would also showcase the relationship better. It is also interesting to note that the x-axis begins the scale at 50%, making the graph seem more extreme. This topic greatly interested me because homicide rates are rising quickly in Mesa, the city where I live. A headline I came up with is: Are Gun Murders Harder to Solve?

I know that Chicago has a large gun trafficking problem along with a high crime rate (mainly gun related), despite them having the strictest gun laws in the nation. Something I also noticed was that many of these cities are in the midwest or just not on the coastlines. I think this is because most of those cities are in states with little to no gun laws.

What I also wonder is why so many California cities are listed here. California has very strict gun laws, but most of the cities are below the trend line. Why is that?

This relates to me in my community because it displays that gun related crimes still occur frequently in places with strict gun laws, which tells me that either the law isn't enforced or just isn't working.

Q1. California has many cities that show up on the graph. All of their cities but San Bernardino have over 50% murders cleared. The cities on this graph do not fall under the slope from 80% murder cleared to 90% of murders being from guns. They fall on the upper diagonal of the graph. They don't also fall in the upper right corner quadrant of the graph with 90%-100% of murders with guns and 80%-100% of murders cleared. Most of the cities lie in the range  of 40%-80% of murders being clear, but also a high rate of 80%-90% of murders with guns. 
Q2. I wonder how many of those places have gun laws especially in places that fall in the top 90%-100%. Is gun control a problem in any of these cities? How do these numbers on either axis correlate with how safe these cities are?
Q3. I think this relates to my community with a recent gun crime making the news. For example, the shooting of Iremamber Sykap that occurred in April of this year, was a case where 16–year-old Iremamber was shot and killed through the rear view mirror of the car he stole at an intersection. This one made the news because even though we knew what had happened to some degree, the officers were not going to go to trial at first. Honolulu, where I reside in, is not a very gun crazy place, with an average of 37% of homicides involving a gun, however, when cases like this make it only the news, it does call attention to those in blue carrying guns. 
Q4. Is your city guncrazy or are they just happy to solve murders?

comments.raw_comment: Something I noticed is that Chicago wasn't labeled on the graph. Chicago has some of the strictest gun laws in the nation, yet over 90% of murders in Chicago are gun murders. Chicago is almost on the trend line, with just under 60% of the murders solved. The graph demonstrates that gun murders are harder to solve, but ignores the far more important fact that gun control doesn't prevent gun violence. Someone might look at this graph and think, "In order to solve more cases, we need less gun murders, so we need less guns, and therefore we need stricter gun control." However, when you notice that cities like Chicago with strict gun laws still have high violent crime rates, it is apparent that stricter gun control is not the solution. One of the leading predictors of violent crime is rates of fatherless homes. Statistics show that in general, a 10 percent increase in fatherless kids results in a 17 percent increase in juvenile crime. Therefore, while the New York Times implies that less guns mean more solved crimes, and therefore safer cities, guns aren't the problem. The problems are societal. The question shouldn't be "What are the most common weapons in murders?", because people will always find another way to kill each other. The question should be "What can we as a society do to increase the numbers of fathers in homes?" We need to address why people commit murders, and not how.  It is more important to prevent murders than to solve them.
